Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Edward, a 55-year-old counselor, had always prided himself on helping others navigate their emotional struggles. His office was a sanctuary, filled with calming colors and comforting artifacts, yet lately, it felt more like a cage. The walls that had once absorbed the burdens of his clients were now closing in on him, echoing a trauma he could neither explain nor escape. The memory of that day lingered like smoke, a ghost of a man-made disaster that changed everything.

It was late summer when the catastrophic event unfolded. Edward had been attending a community event, a local fair meant to bring people together. Laughter and the scent of cotton candy filled the air, but that joy was shattered in an instant. A sudden explosion tore through the venue, sending a shockwave of panic and chaos. Edward could still hear the screams and see the confusion etched on people's faces. The acrid smell of burnt materials and thick plumes of smoke enveloped him. In the aftermath, he found himself standing among scattered debris, his heartbeat racing as the scent of burnt plastic clung to his nostrils. That day, he became a spectator to horror, and it was a show he could not unsee.

In the months that followed, Edward’s life began to fold in on itself. He noticed that certain smells would trigger an overwhelming sense of dread. A waft of smoke from someone’s barbecue would send him spiraling back to that chaotic scene, his body responding as if the threat were alive and present. Even the faintest hint of something burnt made him feel as though he was back in that moment, where chaos ruled and safety was an illusion. He could often smell the burning long after it had faded, and it haunted him. It made him feel as if he were losing his grip on reality, as his mind replayed vivid snippets of the event, leaving him with feelings that seemed to belong to someone else. It was as though he was watching a movie about another person’s trauma, yet the emotions flooded through him with an intensity that left him breathless.

Edward began to withdraw from his friends. He had once relished their company, but now he found excuses to avoid gatherings, fearing that laughter would remind him of the joy he could no longer feel. He was convinced that if he allowed himself to think about the disaster, he would crumble under the weight of it. So, he monitored his thoughts like a hawk, anxious that a single stray memory could plunge him back into the abyss. His friends, concerned about his absence, reached out, but Edward felt an overwhelming urge to hide. It was safer to be alone, away from the probing questions and the risk of feeling vulnerable again.

At work, he found himself struggling to concentrate, his mind a battleground of thoughts that he didn’t want to confront. The therapy sessions with clients began to feel like an act, each session a performance where he wore a mask of composure. He felt like a fraud, unable to extend the help he once provided so effortlessly. The irony of his situation gnawed at him; how could he guide others toward healing when he was so deeply entrapped in his own suffering? The very tools he offered to his clients—self-reflection, acknowledgment of feelings, and confrontation of fears—now felt like a foreign language.

Edward's body had become an enemy, reacting with a jolt of fear to the most innocuous situations. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, where disaster lurked around every corner. That constant vigilance drained him, leaving him exhausted and isolated. He feared that he would never truly escape the shadow of that day, that he would always be a prisoner of his own mind.

Finally, it was a fleeting moment—a faint scent of smoke wafting through his office during a particularly busy day—that pushed Edward to the brink. It was as if that smell had ignited a fuse, and he realized he could not continue living in this state of constant dread. With a heart heavy with both fear and hope, he took the brave step of reaching out for help. He longed to find a way back to himself, to reconnect with the world and the people he cared about. What frightened him most was the possibility that he might never feel whole again, yet somewhere deep within, a flicker of hope remained. He wanted to reclaim his life, to step out of the shadows of the past and into a future where he could breathe freely once more.
